title: CPSC 541 - Chapter 2: Requirements from the Customer's Perspective

questions.question: Which statement best describes a customer in the context of software requirements?
options: Only the person who directly uses the software
Only the person who pays for the software
Anyone who benefits from, requests, pays for, uses, or receives output from the product
Only the project manager
Only members of the development team
Anyone who writes source code for the product
questions.explanation: The chapter uses a broad definition of customer. Customers can include people who benefit from the product, request or pay for it, use it, or receive its output.

questions.question: Every customer is an important stakeholder in the software project.
questions.explanation: Customers have an interest in or dependence on the intended product and therefore are important stakeholders.

questions.question: A department manager never directly uses a reporting system but receives a weekly report generated by it. According to Chapter 2, can this person still be considered a customer?
questions.explanation: A person who receives and benefits from the product's output can be considered a customer.

questions.question: Why is the customer-developer relationship important?
options: Customers are responsible for writing the source code
Excellent requirements depend heavily on collaboration between customers and developers
Developers should allow customers to make all technical decisions
Customers determine the programming language
Developers do not need requirements when communication is good
Customers are responsible for software testing
questions.explanation: The chapter emphasizes that excellent requirements come from effective collaboration between customers and developers.

questions.question: According to the chapter, excellent software is strongly influenced by which two things?
options: A large budget and a large team
Excellent requirements and well-executed design
Fast programming and minimal documentation
New technology and cloud hosting
Automated testing and artificial intelligence
A short schedule and few stakeholders
questions.explanation: The slides state that excellent software comes from well-executed design and excellent requirements.

questions.question: What is one major cause of dissatisfied customers discussed in Chapter 2?
options: Too many programming languages
Lack of clear communication between customers and developers
Too much testing
Excessive database normalization
Too many servers
Using written requirements
questions.explanation: Poor communication can create misunderstandings between what customers need and what developers build.

questions.question: One role of a requirements analyst is to identify the appropriate customers and listen to their needs before development proceeds.
questions.explanation: The professor emphasizes identifying and listening to customers as an important responsibility of requirements analysts.

questions.question: Which of the following are rights of the software customer? Select all that apply.
options: Expect analysts to speak the customer's language
Expect analysts to learn the customer's business
Expect analysts to document requirements appropriately
Expect analysts to explain requirements work products
Expect analysts to act respectfully and professionally
Require developers to accept every requested change without discussion
questions.explanation: The first five are customer rights. Customers do not have the right to force every change into the project without evaluating its impact.

questions.question: What does it mean when the customer has the right to expect analysts to 'speak your language'?
options: The analyst must use the customer's preferred programming language
The analyst should communicate in understandable business terms instead of unnecessary technical jargon
The analyst must speak every human language
The analyst should only communicate through diagrams
The analyst must allow the customer to write source code
The analyst should avoid asking questions
questions.explanation: Analysts should communicate in language the customer understands rather than expecting customers to understand specialized software terminology.

questions.question: A business analyst spends time learning how a hospital processes patients before defining requirements for a hospital system. Which customer right does this support?
options: Expect analysts to learn the customer's business and objectives
Expect all requirements to remain unchanged
Expect the customer to write the specification
Expect developers to ignore feasibility
Expect immediate implementation
Expect customers to approve source code
questions.explanation: Customers have the right to expect analysts to understand their business domain and objectives.

questions.question: Customers have the right to expect analysts to convert information they provide into written or graphical requirements specifications.
questions.explanation: Translating customer information into useful written or graphical requirements is one of the listed customer rights.

questions.question: Why should analysts explain requirements work products to customers?
options: So customers understand what they are reviewing and agreeing to
So customers can replace developers
So requirements no longer need validation
So developers do not need documentation
So project managers can avoid estimating costs
So source code can be written immediately
questions.explanation: Customers need to understand the requirements artifacts so they can meaningfully review, clarify, and eventually approve them.

questions.question: Which behavior is expected from an analyst when working with customers?
options: Dismiss customer concerns when they are difficult
Be respectful, collaborative, and professional
Avoid proposing alternatives
Make all business decisions for the customer
Refuse to explain technical concepts
Accept every request without evaluation
questions.explanation: Respectful and collaborative behavior is explicitly included in the customer's bill of rights.

questions.question: A customer asks for a complicated feature. The analyst proposes a simpler alternative that meets the same business need. Is this consistent with the customer's bill of rights?
questions.explanation: Customers have the right to hear alternatives for requirements and possible implementations.

questions.question: Customers should be allowed to describe characteristics that would make the product easy and enjoyable to use.
questions.explanation: The customer's bill of rights includes expressing usability characteristics and expectations.

questions.question: Why might an analyst suggest adjusting a requirement so an existing component can be reused?
options: To eliminate all customer requirements
To potentially reduce development effort, time, or cost
To avoid talking to customers
To make requirements ambiguous
To eliminate the need for testing
To prevent future changes
questions.explanation: The slides state that customers should receive opportunities to adjust requirements to permit component reuse.

questions.question: If a customer proposes a change after requirements have been agreed upon, what information should the developer provide?
options: Only whether the developer likes the change
Credible cost and schedule impacts along with possible tradeoffs
Only the new source code
A guarantee that there will be no impact
A new programming language recommendation
Only a new project name
questions.explanation: Customers have the right to understand the realistic cost, schedule, and tradeoff implications of changes.

questions.question: According to the customer's bill of rights, what system should the customer ultimately expect to receive?
options: Any system the developers prefer
A system containing every feature ever requested
A system that satisfies the customer's communicated and agreed-upon needs
A system with the newest technology
A system that never changes
A system requiring no maintenance
questions.explanation: The developers are expected to deliver the needs that were communicated and agreed upon.

questions.question: Which of the following are customer responsibilities? Select all that apply.
options: Educate developers about the business and its terminology
Spend time providing and clarifying requirements
Provide specific and precise information
Make timely requirements decisions
Review requirements documents and prototypes
Avoid communicating changes until the end of the project
questions.explanation: Customers are expected to actively participate throughout requirements development. Changes should be communicated promptly, not hidden.

questions.question: The development team is expected to understand the customer's business without receiving any explanation from the customer.
questions.explanation: Customers have a responsibility to educate developers and analysts about their business and specialized terminology.

questions.question: A customer says, 'I already told you roughly what I want. I don't have time to answer more questions.' Which responsibility is the customer failing to fulfill?
options: Spending necessary time to provide and clarify requirements
Writing the system's source code
Deploying the software
Choosing the database
Performing all testing
Creating the development architecture
questions.explanation: Customers must devote sufficient time to requirements work because requirements are clarified iteratively.

questions.question: Why should customers be specific and precise when describing requirements?
options: To reduce misunderstanding and ambiguity
To make developers work faster regardless of quality
To remove the need for validation
To prevent analysts from documenting requirements
To make all requirements permanent
To eliminate the need for prioritization
questions.explanation: Specific and precise input reduces ambiguity and helps create a shared understanding between customers and developers.

questions.question: Why are timely customer decisions important during requirements engineering?
options: Delayed decisions can prevent the project from moving forward
They allow developers to avoid requirements
They guarantee that requirements never change
They eliminate development costs
They allow customers to control source code
They replace the requirements baseline
questions.explanation: The requirements process often depends on customer decisions. Delays can block development or leave unresolved issues.

questions.question: A developer estimates that a requested feature will require six additional weeks. According to the customer's responsibilities, what should the customer do?
options: Assume the developer is exaggerating
Respect the developer's cost and feasibility assessment and discuss tradeoffs
Demand that it be completed without changing the schedule
Immediately replace the developer
Ignore the estimate
Remove the requirements baseline
questions.explanation: Customers have a responsibility to respect credible assessments of cost and technical feasibility.

questions.question: Who has a responsibility to help establish priorities among requirements, features, and use cases?
options: Only the developers
The customer in collaboration with the development team
Only the tester
Only the database administrator
Only the legal department
Nobody because all requirements have equal priority
questions.explanation: Customers are responsible for helping set realistic priorities so the team knows what is most important.

questions.question: Reviewing requirements documents and evaluating prototypes is part of the customer's responsibilities.
questions.explanation: Customers need to actively review requirements and prototypes so mistakes and misunderstandings can be found early.

questions.question: A customer discovers that a business process has changed. When should the customer communicate the change to the development team?
options: Immediately
After the product is released
Only during final testing
After the developer discovers it independently
At the next annual review
Only if the change is free to implement
questions.explanation: The customer's responsibilities include communicating requirements changes promptly.

questions.question: Why should customers follow the project's defined change process?
options: To prevent all requirements from changing
To ensure changes are evaluated, tracked, and incorporated in a controlled way
To allow developers to reject every change
To prevent customers from participating
To eliminate cost estimates
To avoid establishing a baseline
questions.explanation: A controlled change process prevents requirements changes from creating unmanaged cost, schedule, and scope problems.

questions.question: What is one common problem with requirements signoff?
options: Customers may approve requirements they have not carefully read or understood
Requirements automatically disappear after signoff
Developers are no longer allowed to communicate with customers
All testing must occur before signoff
The product must already be finished
Customers become responsible for programming
questions.explanation: The slides warn that customers sometimes sign requirements specifications without actually reading and understanding them.

questions.question: Another signoff problem occurs when developers treat an approved requirements specification as:
options: A temporary draft with no importance
Something permanently fixed that can never change
A source-code repository
A testing document only
A financial report
A user manual
questions.explanation: The chapter warns against treating the signed specification as 'cast in stone.' Requirements will change.

questions.question: It is realistic to expect that every requirement will be completely known before development begins.
questions.explanation: The slides explicitly state that all requirements cannot possibly be known that early and that requirements will change.

questions.question: What is a requirements baseline?
options: A temporary conversation between customer and developer
A snapshot of a stable, controlled, agreed-upon set of requirements
A list of future programming languages
A collection of rejected requirements
A source code backup
A testing benchmark
questions.explanation: The baseline converts fluid work-in-progress into an agreed-upon and controlled specification at a particular point in time.

questions.question: What does establishing a baseline do to requirements work that was previously fluid and changing?
options: Deletes it
Turns it into a stable, controlled, agreed-upon specification
Makes it impossible to change
Converts it into source code
Moves it directly into testing
Makes the customer responsible for implementation
questions.explanation: A baseline creates an agreed reference point from which future requirements changes can be managed.

questions.question: After a baseline is established, requirements may still change.
questions.explanation: A baseline does not freeze requirements forever. Changes are still possible but must be managed.

questions.question: After a baseline is established, a customer requests several major new features. What must the customer understand?
options: The changes must always be free
Changes can require renegotiation of cost, schedule, functionality, or scope
The baseline must be ignored
Developers are obligated to work overtime
The changes automatically replace existing requirements
The project deadline can never move
questions.explanation: Changes after the baseline can affect project commitments and may require tradeoffs or renegotiation.

questions.question: What should the developer understand about an established requirements baseline?
options: It is merely a suggestion
It represents a promise to perform according to the agreed requirements
It eliminates the customer's involvement
It replaces the project schedule
It prevents all future changes
It applies only to testers
questions.explanation: The slides describe the baseline as a commitment by the developer to deliver the agreed-upon product.

questions.question: Why does a requirements baseline increase stakeholder confidence?
options: It guarantees that no software defects will exist
It gives stakeholders a controlled agreement about scope and how changes will be handled
It guarantees an unlimited budget
It prevents users from requesting changes
It eliminates the requirements process
It allows developers to ignore customers
questions.explanation: The baseline provides a shared reference point and helps prevent uncontrolled changes and misunderstandings.

questions.question: Which stakeholder confidence benefits are associated with having a requirements baseline? Select all that apply.
options: Customer managers gain confidence that scope will not grow uncontrollably
Users gain confidence that developers are working toward the right system
Development managers gain confidence that customers will consider cost, schedule, and functionality tradeoffs
Analysts gain confidence that requirements changes will not create uncontrolled chaos
Developers are guaranteed that requirements will never change
Customers no longer need to participate in requirements work
questions.explanation: The chapter presents the baseline as a way to create confidence among customer managers, users, development managers, and analysts while still allowing controlled change.
